slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 3: Managing Resources with RAII. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.title: 3.1 Understanding Resources Beyond Memory
keyPoints: A resource is something whose acquisition creates a corresponding obligation: release a file, unlock a mutex.
Memory is only one example.
Ownership must identify which object performs that release and whether responsibility can be copied or transferred.
A resource is something whose acquisition creates a corresponding obligation: release a file, unlock a mutex.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 3, treat 3.1 Understanding Resources Beyond Memory as a design decision with costs and evidence. A resource is something whose acquisition creates a corresponding obligation: release a file, unlock a mutex, return a buffer, or close a native handle. Memory is only one example. Ownership must identify which object performs that release and whether responsibility can be copied or transferred. RAII is a lifetime technique, not an assurance that every possible external failure becomes recoverable. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 3, treat 3.1.2 Associating Resources with Object Lifetime as a design decision with costs and evidence. An automatic wrapper is destroyed when its scope exits normally and during applicable exception unwinding. That makes cleanup compose across helper functions: each local owner is responsible for its own resource, rather than an outer catch block guessing which partial operations succeeded. Lifetime-based cleanup does not run after every possible process termination mechanism or hardware failure. It also cannot prove that buffered data reached durable storage. Separate resource release, successful output completion, and durability requirements. A file destructor closing a stream is not a substitute for a reviewed persistence protocol. slides.title: 3.2.2 Releasing Resources During Destruction
keyPoints: The destructor attempts cleanup without throwing.
Since close can itself fail, the explicit close() method returns whether the operation succeeded and first removes.
A destructor cannot conveniently report a late write failure to a caller that has already committed success.
A destructor is a poor place for a recoverable error conversation.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 3, treat 3.2.2 Releasing Resources During Destruction as a design decision with costs and evidence. The destructor attempts cleanup without throwing. Since close can itself fail, the explicit close() method returns whether the operation succeeded and first removes the stored ownership claim so a later destructor will not close the same handle twice. A destructor cannot conveniently report a late write failure to a caller that has already committed success. Therefore code with a meaningful output-completion requirement should explicitly finish or close and check before reporting success. The destructor remains the fallback for failure paths. After explicit close, the raw borrowed handle returned by get() is no longer usable; the interface is intentionally narrow and its precondition must be respected. keyPoints: Draw four states for the temporary-file wrapper: not yet constructed, open, explicitly closed, and destroyed.

get() borrows the open handle but does not change ownership.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 3, treat Trace acquisition, use, completion, and fallback as a design decision with costs and evidence. Draw four states for the temporary-file wrapper: not yet constructed, open, explicitly closed, and destroyed. Successful construction moves from the first state to open. get() borrows the open handle but does not change ownership. Explicit close transitions to closed even if its completion result reports a failure. Destruction of an open owner attempts release; destruction of a closed owner has no handle left to release. The worked test writes a known byte sequence, seeks to the beginning, reads back bytes, and checks their content before closing explicitly. These are independent checks. A correct write count does not prove the seek worked, and a matching prefix does not prove the expected number of bytes was read. Keep the evidence attached to the operation it validates. slides.title: Failure clinic — The destructor that never ran
keyPoints: A novice places a raw handle in an enclosing object and expects that object’s destructor to clean it up if later.
The expectation is wrong when the enclosing constructor never completed.
The repair is not another broad catch in every caller.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 3, treat Failure clinic — The destructor that never ran as a design decision with costs and evidence. A novice places a raw handle in an enclosing object and expects that object’s destructor to clean it up if later constructor work throws. The expectation is wrong when the enclosing constructor never completed. The repair is not another broad catch in every caller. Put the handle into a completed RAII member or a local owner before beginning the later work, so a completed subobject has the release obligation. A second failure arises when a wrapper is copied. Both copies contain the same handle, and both destructors attempt release. Suppressing one destructor call manually merely moves the uncertainty elsewhere. Delete copy operations when exclusive ownership is intended, and later add a move operation that empties the source deliberately. A raw address copy and an ownership transfer are different operations. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

Use the supplied resource-audit laboratory in Appendix B to study cleanup without depending on a real device. The fake resource has a small handle number, a live-handle registry, and a release counter. Its owner is noncopyable and movable. The registry outlives all owners, so observations do not dangle. There is no global handle allocator or external service to make the test nondeterministic. Test successful acquisition and scope exit first. Then throw a distinct controlled exception after acquisition and verify that the registry is empty after the catch. Attempt failed acquisition and verify that no release is recorded for a resource that never existed. Move an owner and confirm that the original no longer releases the transferred handle. Close explicitly twice and verify that the second call changes no counters.
